A perfect partition in this paper is an axis-parallel dissection of a rectangle into at least two
pairwise noncongruent rectangles of equal positive area. Congruence allows a quarter-turn. This
paper supplies complete versions of the boundary and search arguments used by Garc ´ ıa-Col ´ ın,

computations. No universal nonexistence assertion follows here.
Theorem 1(Source Lemma 2.1).A perfect partition has at least seven pieces, even if their side
lengths are real.
Proof.Suppose otherwise and choose such a partition with the least numberrof pieces. There
cannot be two pieces: they would have equal widths or equal heights and, by equality of area,
would be congruent. No piece spans an entire width or height of the container. Removing such
a piece leaves one or two nonempty rectangular regions. A region consisting of one piece would
make that piece congruent to the removed spanning piece. Every remaining region therefore
contains at least two pieces and is a smaller perfect partition, contradicting minimality. Each
container side therefore meets at least two pieces along intervals of positive length, and the four
corner pieces are distinct.
Suppose each side meets exactly two pieces. These must be its corner pieces, so only the
four corner pieces meet the boundary. Scale the two coordinate axes independently to make the
container the unit square. This scaling is used only to derive equality of the widths and heights
of two pieces, which remains an equality on undoing the scaling. The common normalized area

Some side consequently meetsk≥3 pieces. Take this as the bottom side. The heights of
these pieces are pairwise distinct: equal heights and equal areas would force congruence. None
reaches the top. Each has at least one piece immediately above its upper edge, and these sets
of upper neighbors are mutually disjoint, since an upper neighbor’s bottom coordinate is the
height of the corresponding bottom piece. They also contain no bottom piece. The lowest
bottom piece has at least two upper neighbors. Otherwise its unique upper neighbor covers its
full top edge. At each endpoint, either the container wall or the adjacent, strictly taller bottom
piece prevents horizontal extension, so this neighbor has exactly the same width. Equal area
again gives congruence. There are therefore at leastk+ (k+ 1)≥7 pieces.
Lemma 2(Integral positions).In an axis-parallel tiling with integer piece widths and heights,
every piece corner has integer coordinates relative to a container corner.

Proof.Choose a horizontal line through the interior of a particular vertical piece edge, avoiding
all horizontal piece edges. The segments into which the tiling partitions this line have the integer
widths of the pieces it crosses. Every endpoint’s horizontal coordinate is their partial sum from
the left wall. A vertical line gives the analogous conclusion for horizontal edges.

Lemma 4(Choice of uncovered valley).The exact search may instead choose any maximal flat
skyline interval whose neighbors have strictly larger covered heights, with container walls allowed
as neighbors. In particular it may choose such an interval with fewest currently fitting shapes
and orientations.
Proof.Let the interval be [x, x+w) at heighty. In a completion, the piece covering its leftmost
lowest uncovered unit cell cannot begin belowy, since that would overlap the covered region.
It cannot extend to the left because of the wall or the strictly higher neighboring column. It
therefore begins at (x, y). It cannot cross the strictly higher right neighbor either. Thus its entire
base lies in this flat interval and is one of the legal choices. Each placement still preserves the
skyline invariant. Induction on the remaining pieces proves completeness for any deterministic
selection of such an interval. A lowest interval always exists until completion.
Proposition 5(Safe necessary prunings).The following conditions may be required at every
partial skyline state without losing any completion:
1. each remaining open component separated by full-height columns has area a multiple ofA;
2. the width of every lowest uncovered plateau is the sum of widths of a subset of distinct
unused shapes in fitting orientations;
3. the four container sides admit side subsets with their exact lengths; adjacent subsets share
exactly their common corner piece, and opposite subsets can share only pieces spanning
the intervening container dimension.
For a square, one may additionally require that its bottom-left corner piece has least unordered
shape index among all four corner pieces, and that this piece has width at most height. Repeated
corner identities must be allowed.
Proof.An unplaced rectangle cannot cross a full-height column, so the first assertion follows by
summing equal areas within a component. The pieces starting along a lowest plateau partition

its base interval and have distinct unused shapes, proving the second assertion. The third follows
by reading the boundary of an actual tiling; a rectangle meeting two opposite sides spans the
intervening width or height. Finally the dihedral symmetries of a square can send a least corner
piece to the bottom left. Reflection in the diagonal through that corner then chooses its width
at most its height. A piece spanning a dimension may occupy two corners, which is why the
least-index inequalities are non-strict.
Proposition 6(Parity endpoint constraint).In any integer tiling, take the parity of the number
of uncovered unit cells on each horizontal row of a partial placement. Every remaining rectan-
gle of odd width contributes the indicator of its vertical interval, and rectangles of even width
contribute zero. Thus the discrete derivative of the uncovered parity profile is the symmetric
difference of the endpoint pairs of the remaining odd-width intervals. The analogous assertion
holds for columns and odd heights. Also, the alternating column sum of the uncovered cells is
the sum of±hover remaining odd-width pieces, and the alternating row sum is the sum of±w
over remaining odd-height pieces.
Proof.Reduce the width contributions on a row modulo two and then take differences between
consecutive rows, including the two exterior zero rows. An interval’s indicator changes exactly
at its two endpoints. For the alternating sum, the sum of (−1) x along an integer interval is zero
for even length and is 1 or−1 for odd length. Sum over the height of each rectangle. Columns
are dual.
